name: Salt marsh
notes: Tidal grassland of salt-tolerant cordgrasses, rushes and succulent glasswort, zoned from the daily-flooded low marsh to a high marsh of salt hay, sea lavender and marsh elder; drawn on the US Atlantic/Gulf coast marshes and NW European (Wadden Sea, UK) saltings.

traits.native_range: Pinus taeda, loblolly pine, southeastern US coastal plain, mixed with live oak in maritime forest, 25-35 m — USDA Plants
traits.leaf_shape: needles or scale leaves, evergreen (larch deciduous)
traits.trunk: single straight trunk, whorled branches, conical crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: rounded crown high on a long straight trunk

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 5-8 cotyledons and single primary needles, then slender needles in bundles of three. Fast saplings add several growth flushes a year, forming open, fairly narrow cones with long, soft, yellow-green needles and a strong leader; older trees self-prune into tall, clear trunks with rounded crowns.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Baker & Langdon): germination from March at 18-27 C; site index ~27 m at 50 years on average sites; stands of 25 years can reseed, 40-year-olds bear 3-5 times more; moderately tolerant when young, intolerant with age; medium-lived, max recorded 245 years

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (flowers Feb 15-Apr 10; cones 7.5-15 cm, light reddish-brown when mature, ripe by the second October after flowering, ~26 months after the strobili are initiated; seedfall Oct-early Dec); crop and decay estimated

canopy.name: Mangrove buckthorn
canopy.origin: Gulf coast, Mexico and the Caribbean

growth.juvenile_note: A seedling from a bird-dropped stone: a wiry stem with small, leathery, spoon-shaped grey-green leaves. It branches early and stiffly at wide angles, each short side shoot ending in a sharp thorn, and becomes a dense, tangled, thorny shrub before one or a few stems lift it into a small, crooked tree.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 8 (Sideroxylon celastrinum: shrubs or trees to 9 m, branches thorn-tipped; coastal thickets, shell ridges and salt marsh edges, S Texas and S Florida); germination, growth and ages estimated

canopy.source: Sideroxylon celastrinum (syn. Bumelia celastrina), saffron plum / mangrove buckthorn, S Texas and S Florida to Mexico and the Caribbean, thorny shrub or tree to 9 m of coastal thickets and the upper edge of salt marshes and mangroves — Flora of North America vol. 8; Kew POWO (accepted)

bark.notes: grey, smooth on young stems, shallowly fissured on old trunks; twigs stiff, ending in thorns

leaf.notes: small leathery obovate to spoon-shaped leaves, alternate or crowded on short spur shoots beside the thorns

flower.form: tiny fragrant greenish-white bell flowers in clusters along the twigs

appearance.silhouette: crooked thorny thicket-tree at the marsh's landward edge
appearance.refs: Flora of North America vol. 8; USDA PLANTS Sideroxylon celastrinum

leaf.note: obovate to spatulate, leathery, glabrous, often fascicled on spur shoots

fruiting.source: Flora of North America vol. 8 (small greenish-white flowers in axillary fascicles; drupes ellipsoid, purple-black); fruit eaten by birds and mammals and by people; phenology window, set and crop estimated

bark.note: grey-brown, shallowly fissured on old stems; young twigs green and angled

shrub.silhouette: rounded grey-green bush, white-fluffed in autumn

growth.juvenile_note: Wind-blown achenes sprout on bare, damp ground within 1-3 weeks. The seedling has two small oval cotyledons, then thick, grey-green, coarsely toothed, wedge-shaped leaves on a single stem that branches in its first year; the young plant is an upright, leafy, many-branched bush, often flowering in its second autumn.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 4 m, dioecious, snowy-white cottony female heads in autumn, nectar for butterflies including monarchs, seeds toxic); weed-management literature (Queensland, CABI) on quick light-dependent germination, flowering from year 2 and seed output; lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (autumn flowering, female heads become snowy-white tufts, seeds toxic); weed literature (a large female bush sheds up to ~1.5 million plumed achenes); heads-per-plant, fruit set and timings estimated. Counts are flower heads.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings come up in spring along the upper marsh edge and wrack line: a slender stem with pairs of thick, fleshy, toothed, lance-shaped leaves. It grows quickly into a many-branched, semi-woody shrub whose upper branches carry leafy spikes of small, nodding, greenish-white flower heads in late summer.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Iva frutescens: shrub to 3.5 m, many small heads with whitish florets, narrow band at the upper salt-marsh margin, growth limited by flooding); wind pollination as in other Iva; timings estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (elongated arrays of many small whitish heads); Iva heads are wind-pollinated and set small dark obovoid achenes shed through autumn and winter (timings, set and crop estimated).

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with small oval cotyledons, then narrow, aromatic, olive-green leaves toothed near the tip and dotted with tiny amber resin glands, as in the adult. It soon branches from the base into a dense, twiggy evergreen bush; nitrogen-fixing root nodules let it grow fast (often ~1 m a year) on poor sand, and it spreads by root sprouts into thickets.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 14 m; dioecious catkins late winter-spring; waxy globular fruit in late summer-fall; birds strip the wax, needed for germination); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Myrica (small waxy dry drupes persisting over winter; no endosperm); growth and ages estimated

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (dioecious, wind-pollinated catkins late winter-spring; fruit ripe late summer-fall, globular with a pale blue-grey wax coat, used for bayberry candles); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Myrica (tiny dry waxy drupes that persist on the shrub over winter); set and crop estimated

shrub.name: Sea oxeye
shrub.origin: SE US, Mexico and Caribbean coasts

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are uncommon; most new plants are shoots from the running rhizomes of an existing colony. A young shoot is a single upright stem with pairs of thick, silvery-grey, hairy, spoon-shaped leaves; it branches little, turns woody at the base and is soon one of many stems in a dense, knee- to waist-high grey patch topped by yellow daisies.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 21 (Borrichia frutescens: rhizomatous colonial shrub 10-120(-200) cm; leaves opposite, obovate to oblanceolate, sericeous; heads solitary, rays yellow; salt marshes, mangrove margins and coastal flats); establishment mostly clonal; timings estimated.

repro.note: spreads mainly by rhizomes into clonal colonies; heads visited by bees and butterflies; the corky achenes float

shrub.source: Borrichia frutescens, sea oxeye: silvery-leaved colonial subshrub 0.3-1.2 m of salt-marsh edges, mangrove margins and salt flats, Virginia to Texas, Mexico, Bermuda and the West Indies — Flora of North America vol. 21; Odum et al. 1982 (landward mangrove fringe). Kew POWO for the name.

fruit.form: dark brown, stiff, prickly-chaffed seed heads that persist on the dead stems

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.note: terete dark grey-green leaves and culms; brown basal sheaths

growth.juvenile_note: Light-requiring seeds germinate on open sandy mud; the seedling is a thin, dark-green, needle-sharp tuft that spreads by rhizome into a dense stand of stiff, grey-green to blackish, spine-tipped leaves. Each leaf-shoot lives a year or two, then stands dead and grey for years, giving the marsh its dark 'black rush' colour; the clonal stands themselves persist for decades.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Juncus roemerianus: over 2 m at low salinity, under 30 cm at high; spreads by rhizome; seeds need light and fail under mud; seedlings mainly on open sand; new shoots all year, dead leaves persist). Lifespan is for the clump (each leaf-shoot lives ~1-2 yr); timings estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: one soft shoot with flat, tapering, bright-green leaves; it tillers within weeks and sends out rhizomes, reaching ~15 cm in 3-4 months and a small tuft of spongy stems by autumn. Each culm lives about a year (north: dies back in autumn), but the rhizome clone spreads up to 3 m a season and persists for decades.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Spartina alterniflora (germinates Apr-Jun, flowers Jun-Oct, 0.4-2.5 m, shoots die back in autumn); USDA NRCS Cape May PMC Plant Guide (most seed germinates in 7-10 d after 1-4 months cold-wet storage; ~15 cm in 3-4 months; 2.5-3 m lateral spread per season; cover in 2-3 seasons)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are rare (germination is episodic, needing fresh water on saline ground); the seedling is a small tuft of short, stiff, grey-green leaves in two neat opposite ranks. Scaly rhizomes then run through the soil and send up rows of short, stiff, leafy shoots, forming a dense, low turf patch; male and female plants are separate.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Distichlis spicata (dioecious; seeds need stratification and scarification, germination rare and episodic, seedling survival 0-95% with falling salinity; rhizomes to 180 cm long, 10-25 cm deep; 15-45 cm tall, usually <30 cm; photosynthesis rises with light). Time to flowering and clone lifespan estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a hair-thin shoot with wiry, inrolled leaves, emerging in May; it tillers and sends thin rhizomes into a small dense tuft, with no flowers in year one and only a few in year two. Mature stands are a dense turf of fine, wiry stems that lodge into swirled 'cowlicks'.
growth.source: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board written findings 1999 (seedlings emerge in May, do not flower in first season, few flowers in second; flowers Jun-Sep; spreads mainly by rhizomes); USDA NRCS plant guides (rhizomatous, mostly under 1 m); FEIS Spartina patens

ground.name: Common orange lichen

growth.juvenile_note: Begins as a speck of orange granules where a spore met its green alga on nutrient-rich bark or stone. It spreads outward a few millimetres a year as a rosette of flat, crinkled, overlapping lobes 1-4 mm wide, bright orange-yellow in sun and greyish-green in shade, soon crowded in the middle with little orange cup-shaped fruit bodies.
growth.source: British Lichen Society and Wikipedia (Xanthoria parietina: foliose rosettes to about 10 cm, lobes 1-4 mm, orange apothecia, greener in shade; favours nitrogen-rich bark and stone); radial growth of a few mm a year from lichenometric studies; lifespan estimated

repro.note: spores from the orange cups must meet a free green alga; no flowers

ground.source: Xanthoria parietina, common orange lichen, nearly cosmopolitan, on nutrient-rich bark of palms, tamarisk and fig and on walls and stones, North Africa and Arabia included; foliose rosettes to 10 cm of flat orange-yellow lobes with orange cups, greener in shade — British Lichen Society / Wikipedia

leaf.notes: rosettes of flat crinkled lobes 1-4 mm wide, bright orange-yellow, pale beneath, crowded with orange cups in the middle

appearance.seasonal: brighter orange in full sun, grey-green in shade
appearance.silhouette: bright orange rosettes splashed on bark and stone
